source: Deng et al. (2023/2024) PentestGPT
finding: Plain LLMs do well on single pentest sub-tasks but lose the whole-test context. A three-module scaffold (reasoning tree, generation, parsing) fixes part of this.
numbers: Benchmark 13 targets, 182 sub-tasks. Plain GPT-3.5 1/13 targets, 23.07% sub-tasks; GPT-4 5/13 (38.46%), 52.20% sub-tasks; Bard 2/13, 27.47%. Hard targets: 0/2 for all plain models.
limits: Custom benchmark, small N, human in loop; hard targets unsolved by every setup.
agent_relevance: Context loss over a long red-team run is the main failure; an external task tree held by code is the fix, matching our program-owns-state rule (G1/G2).

source: Deng et al. (2023/2024) PentestGPT scaffold gain
finding: Scaffold beat naive use of the same model. Authors report scaffold gains on sub-tasks and more medium targets.
numbers: Sub-task completion +228.6% over GPT-3.5 and +58.6% over GPT-4 (abstract/intro). PentestGPT-GPT-4 57 vs naive GPT-4 27 sub-tasks on one comparison (+111%). Real targets: 4 of 10 HackTheBox/picoMini challenges solved.
limits: Relative gains on a small base; authors still need a human in the loop; hard targets still fail.
agent_relevance: Structure around the model, not a bigger model, produced the gain. Supports the scaffold-over-training premise.

source: Deng et al. (2023/2024) PentestGPT limits
finding: Authors state LLMs hallucinate and have outdated knowledge; task-tree verification helps but does not remove errors; a human in the loop stays vital.
numbers: Hard targets: 0 of 2 solved by every tool variant.
limits: Qualitative statement from authors.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G2: revisions must come from real tool output, not model opinion.

source: Isozaki et al. (2024/2025) Towards Automated Penetration Testing baseline
finding: Open benchmark of 13 machines. Neither GPT-4o nor Llama 3.1-405B could finish a single machine end to end with PentestGPT, even with minimal human help.
numbers: Benchmark: 13 boxes, 72 tasks. Easy recon 47.6% (10/21) GPT-4o vs 57.1% (12/21) Llama. Hard recon 20.0% both. Privilege escalation: GPT-4o 12.5%, Llama 0%. Llama beat GPT-4o on 7 machines, tied 4, lost 2.
limits: Small N per cell (1-21 tasks); prompts tuned on one box (WestWild); Llama run at 8K context.
agent_relevance: End-to-end autonomous red teaming of real machines is not solved by a base model plus a tool wrapper.

source: Isozaki et al. (2024/2025) Towards Automated Penetration Testing ablations
finding: Three stacked ablations on Llama 3.1-405B: (1) summary of summaries, (2) structured to-do list instead of free-text tree, (3) RAG over HackTricks. Summary injection helped exploitation; RAG plus structure helped enumeration and privilege escalation; the structured list alone hurt Symfonos 2 enumeration because the model added every suid binary and ignored removal.
numbers: Only two boxes ablated (Funbox, Symfonos 2). Funbox privilege escalation 0/1 baseline to 1/1 with to-do list; Symfonos 2 privilege escalation 0/1 to 1/1 only with RAG. Task counts 1-8 per cell.
quote: if we make the remove task tool too aggressive, it does remove useful tasks
limits: Tiny samples, one run each; authors say the structure benefit is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Memory summaries and retrieval plausibly help long-horizon red-team loops; a mutable task list needs a code-controlled remove rule. Weak evidence [S].

source: Isozaki et al. (2024/2025) Towards Automated Penetration Testing forgetting
finding: Performance falls in later steps because each module sees only the past 5 exchanges; GPT-4o forgot SSH existed by the time credentials were found.
numbers: Context of last 5 exchanges per module; later-step success lower in their figures (exact values not extracted).
limits: Hypothesis checked by ablation on two boxes only.
agent_relevance: Long-run forgetting is a concrete failure; keep a code-held fact ledger.

source: Muzsai et al. (2024) HackSynth benchmark
finding: Planner plus Summarizer agent on 200 CTF challenges (PicoCTF 120, OverTheWire 80). GPT-4o best.
numbers: GPT-4o solved 41/120 PicoCTF and 32/80 OverTheWire. Llama-3.1-70B 27/120 PicoCTF and 23/80 OverTheWire; beat GPT-4o-mini on OverTheWire.
limits: CTF challenges are not full red-team engagements; one config per model.
agent_relevance: Gives a measured ceiling for a simple planner-summarizer loop in 2024.

source: Muzsai et al. (2024) HackSynth temperature
finding: Performance flat from temperature 0 to 1, then falls. Command error rate rises above 1. Above 1.6 commands damage the environment; at 2 the system was unusable before 100 challenges.
numbers: Fixed at temperature 1, top-p 0.9 for main runs. Prompt-chaining cut performance 5% and added 17% time; larger observation window helped up to a point (250 for PicoCTF, 500 for OverTheWire).
limits: Noisy curves; two small models used for tuning.
agent_relevance: Sampling temperature is a safety knob in an agent that acts: unchecked high-entropy action drift breaks the environment. Argument for code-checked actions.

source: Muzsai et al. (2024) HackSynth safety
finding: Agent may hallucinate target IPs and attack out-of-scope systems or modify host files. Authors say safeguards are essential.
numbers: Qualitative; no rate given in the pages read.
limits: Discussion section.
agent_relevance: A scope guard (allow-list) must be code, not prompt.

source: Kong et al. (2025) VulnBot
finding: Multi-agent split into recon, scan, exploit roles with a penetration task graph and memory. Beats base models and PentestGPT on AutoPenBench.
numbers: VulnBot-Llama3.1-405B 30.3% overall completion and 69.05% sub-task completion; base Llama3.1-405B 9.09% overall, GPT-4o 21.21% overall (as quoted in text).
limits: Authors own comparison, 5 runs; real-world category only 18.18% for the Llama 3.3-70B variant.
agent_relevance: Role decomposition mirroring a human red team is measurable. Check whether the gain is architecture or just more calls.

source: Luong et al. (2026) xOffense
finding: A fine-tuned mid-size model (Qwen3-32B) inside a three-agent pipeline beats a 405B model in its native setup.
numbers: AutoPenBench sub-task completion 79.17% (251) fine-tuned vs 52.36% (166) base Qwen3-32B vs 69.05% Llama3.1-405B (VulnBot paper). Real-world category 35.96% fine-tuned vs 24.92% base vs 26.19% Llama3.1-405B.
limits: Sub-task counted as success if solved in any of five runs, which flatters all systems; run protocols differ across papers.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning and scaffold are confounded; see the baseline-first paper.

source: Ginige et al. (2025) AutoPentester
finding: Iterative agent that picks tools from earlier findings. Compared with PentestGPT on HackTheBox and custom VMs.
numbers: 27.0% higher sub-task completion, 39.5% more vulnerability coverage, fewer steps; expert survey score 3.93 out of 5, 19.8% above PentestGPT.
limits: Small VM set; subjective expert survey.
agent_relevance: Experts rated report quality; a form of white-cell scoring.

source: Dhakal et al. (2026) Baselines Before Architecture plain agents
finding: Controlled study on the 104-task XBOW benchmark. Three default coding CLI agents with the same GPT-5 and budget: Codex best.
numbers: Pass@1: Codex 70/104, OpenCode 57, Pi 58. Pass@2 union Codex 81, OpenCode 67, Pi 65. Codex vs OpenCode p=0.015, vs Pi p=0.023. Codex about 2.3x cost per run, $27.71 vs $11.93 and $12.00.
limits: Single benchmark; only two passes per condition.
agent_relevance: Strong check on our own claims: a plain agent with a strong model already solves most of the set.

source: Dhakal et al. (2026) Baselines Before Architecture prompts
finding: Adding security-specific prompt text did not help; the shipped default prompt was best.
numbers: Codex GPT-5: native default 70/70 first/second pass (P@2 81); detailed task prompt 64/58 (P@2 68); whole-system prompt 60/68 (P@2 75). Cost per run about $32 for prompted vs $27.71 default. Table text garbled by PDF extraction; row matching inferred.
limits: Two passes per condition; no significance test seen for this table.
agent_relevance: Negative result for domain prompts. Matches G4 and our SCHEMA cautions.

source: Dhakal et al. (2026) Baselines Before Architecture architecture gap
finding: After matching the model, a plain agent closes most of the gap to published harnesses. The residual shows on single attempts and cost.
numbers: Published PentestGPT V2 GPT-5 76.9% vs plain 67.3% (+9.6 pp, plain P@2 77.9%); GPT-5.2 85.0% vs 79.8% (+5.2 pp, P@2 88.5%). Plain P@2 exceeds the MAPTA published score and exceeds PentestGPT V2 GPT-5.2 by 3.5 pp.
limits: Published numbers come from other labs with other protocols.
agent_relevance: Harness gains shrink as the model improves. Measure scaffold value against a plain-model control.

source: Dhakal et al. (2026) Baselines Before Architecture model scaling
finding: Same Codex scaffold with newer models: big gains from the model alone.
limits: One scaffold; costs repriced by the authors.
agent_relevance: Benchmark saturation is near; harder held-out red-team tasks are needed.

source: Fang et al. (2024) LLM Agents can Autonomously Hack Websites
finding: A GPT-4 agent with tools, documents and planning hacked 15 web vulnerabilities with no prior knowledge of the flaw. Open-source models scored 0%.
numbers: GPT-4 73.3% pass@5 (11 of 15) and 42.7% overall success; GPT-3.5 6.7% (1 of 15), 2.7% overall; every open-source model tested 0%. About $9.81 per success estimate in text.
limits: Sandbox sites only; 15 vulnerabilities; stronger models since.
agent_relevance: Agent plus tools plus planning is enough for offense; a capability scaling trend.

source: Zhu et al. (2024/2025) Teams of LLM Agents can Exploit Zero-Day Vulnerabilities (HPTSA)
finding: A planner agent that launches task-specific sub-agents beat a single agent on unknown (zero-day) flaws. Scanners found none.
numbers: HPTSA with GPT-4: 42% pass@5, 18% pass@1 on post-cutoff real vulnerabilities; 4.3x a single GPT-4 no-description agent at pass@1 and 2.0x at pass@5; within 1.8x of an agent given the vulnerability. ZAP and Metasploit 0%.
limits: Small benchmark; GPT-4 only for the best result; open models refuse (31% for one Llama).
agent_relevance: A generalist plans and specialists attack, like a red cell. Ablations say expert agents and documents are necessary.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cybench
finding: 40 professional CTF tasks, 8 models. Unguided, models only solved tasks that humans solved in up to 11 minutes first-solve time.
numbers: Structured bash agent unguided (1 attempt): Claude 3.5 Sonnet 17.5%, GPT-4o 12.5%, Claude 3 Opus 10.0%, o1-preview 10.0%, Llama 3.1-405B 7.5%, Mixtral 7.5%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 7.5%, Llama 3-70B 5.0%. Subtask performance 43.9% Claude 3.5, 46.8% o1-preview. Hardest task human first-solve 24h54m (747x the easiest).
limits: Single attempt in Table 2; 3 attempts in Table 3 raise the best to about 20%.
agent_relevance: Gives a human-time yardstick. Models fail on long multi-step tasks, like long-horizon reasoning.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Cybench scaffold and guidance
finding: Subtask guidance and scaffold change results unevenly and by model.
numbers: Table 3 (3 attempts): unguided 10.0 to 20.0%; subtask-guided 17.5% to 27.5%. Pseudoterminal and web-search scaffold helped Claude 3.5 Sonnet and hurt GPT-4o.
limits: Small task count (40); cells differ by one or two tasks.
agent_relevance: Scaffold effects are model-dependent; test the scaffold per model.

source: Perez et al. (2022) Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
finding: Older foundation: a red LM generates test questions that make a 280B chatbot reply offensively. Zero-shot, few-shot, supervised and RL red LMs compared.
numbers: 0.5M zero-shot test cases: 3.7% offensive replies, 18,444 failures. RL methods most effective; supervised and few-shot raise yield but trade off diversity (Self-BLEU).
limits: Classifier-judged harm only; 2022 model.
agent_relevance: Automated red teaming needs a yield-versus-diversity trade-off; use a code metric for diversity.

source: Heiding et al. (2024) Evaluating LLM Capability to Launch Fully Automated Spear Phishing Campaigns
finding: Social-engineering test on 101 human participants. Fully automated AI phishing matched human experts.
numbers: Click-through: control 12%, human expert 54%, AI automated 54%, AI with human in the loop 56%. Claude 3.5 Sonnet detected 97.25% of 363 phishing emails with no false positives; AI raised phishing profit up to 50 times.
limits: Small N (101); detection result on a different dataset.
agent_relevance: Social break-in tests can now run at machine scale; the blue side can use the same models to detect.

source: Kumarage et al. (2025) SE-VSim and SE-OmniGuard
finding: LLM attacker and LLM victim agents with Big Five traits simulated 1,000+ social-engineering chats. Detectors tested.
numbers: Overall accuracy: GPT-4o zero-shot 0.520, few-shot 0.580, ConvoSentinel GPT-4o 0.680, SE-OmniGuard 0.813; overall F1 SE-OmniGuard 0.815 vs best baseline 0.640.
limits: Simulated victims, not real people; baselines trained per class.
agent_relevance: Red and blue agent pair in simulation; simulated victim traits are untested against humans.

source: Shen et al. (2026) ACEA red versus blue arena
finding: Arena where a red-team adapter and a blue-team adapter face one target LLM, scored by an LLM judge with seeded canonical secrets as ground truth.
numbers: Defense rate can diverge from attributed defense rate: a minimal defense scored 1.000 defense rate but 0.000 attributed because the target refused unaided in all thirty rounds.
quote: the target's own alignment ... determines whether an attack can succeed at all
limits: Platform paper; no large benchmark; LLM judge used.
agent_relevance: Blue credit must be separated from target refusals. Use ground truth (planted secrets) not a judge. Acts like a white cell.

source: Zhuo et al. (2026) CTF-Dojo
finding: 658 containerised CTF tasks for training with verified feedback. 486 execution-verified trajectories raised Qwen3 agents.
numbers: Qwen3-32B Pass@1 averaged 22.0% to 31.9% (+9.9) across InterCode-CTF, NYU CTF Bench and Cybench; Cybench for that model 10.4 (+5.7).
limits: Training approach, not scaffold-only.
agent_relevance: Verifiable flags make a clean reward; relevant to RL on checkable outcomes, not to our no-training plan.

source: Hugglestone et al. (2026) STRIATUM-CTF ablation
finding: Schema-validated tool calls via MCP. 180 runs on 15 CTF challenges under four documentation levels.
numbers: Success 77.8% (minimal docs) to 86.7% (baseline); chi-square(3, N=180)=1.36, p=0.71; Kruskal-Wallis p=0.77. Schema-only already 77.8%.
limits: One live CTF win against 30+ teams is a single event; authors call it feasibility only.
agent_relevance: Typed, code-validated tool calls carried the result; extra documentation did not significantly add. Supports code-checked actions.

source: Microsoft (2025) DefenderBench
finding: Blue-team benchmark: network intrusion, malicious content, code vulnerability, cybersecurity knowledge.
numbers: DefenderBench score: Claude-3.7-sonnet 81.65, Claude-3.7-sonnet-think 78.40, Llama 3.3 70B 71.81 (best open-weight).
limits: Aggregate score; task mix chosen by authors.
agent_relevance: The defender side is measured too; extended thinking did not beat the non-thinking run here.
